extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical arithmetic/geometry (readers of historical mathematical treatises)
extracted.subtask_description: An exposition on continued (chain) proportional quantities: definitions, algebraic and geometric methods to construct intermediate means, rules for multiplying and extending proportional sequences, and properties involving squares/cubes and sums. The text gives procedural rules and numeric examples for manipulating continued proportional magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — continued (chain) proportional quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Four or more quantities are in continued proportion when each consecutive ratio equals the next; i.e., first:second = second:third = third:fourth (and so on).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the fundamental definition used throughout: when a sequence is continued-proportional, relations such as b^2 = a·c (for four terms a,b,c,d with a:b = b:c = c:d) follow. The text repeatedly uses this equality of consecutive ratios as the starting criterion for all subsequent constructions and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean proportional construction via product and root
rubrics_metrics.description: To find a mean proportional between two given quantities, multiply the extremes and extract the appropriate root (square root for one mean, cube root for two means, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example idea from text: if a, x, c are in continued proportion (a:x = x:c), then x is the mean proportional and satisfies x^2 = a·c, so x = sqrt(a·c). For finding two intermediate means between extremes one uses the cube root of the product of extremes. The treatise emphasizes algebraic extraction of roots (arithmetical) and also geometric methods to obtain these means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicative generation and preservation of proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplying every term of a continued-proportional sequence by the same factor (or by systematic integer factors) produces another continued-proportional sequence; similarly, taking certain multiples/doublings/quadruplings of terms preserves proportional relations in predictable ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives many numeric examples (powers of 2, 4, 8, etc.) to show how multiplying terms yields new proportional sequences and how doubling/quadrupling correspond to moving along powers. For instance, multiplying terms appropriately can create sequences whose ratios are preserved and which generate larger tables of proportional quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic consequences for squares and cubes in continued proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: If terms are continued-proportional, then relations among squares and cubes of terms hold (e.g., the square of a middle term equals the product of its neighbors; analogous relations for cubes when more means are involved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: for a:b = b:c, b^2 = a·c. For sequences involving third powers (cubes) and multiple intermediate terms, corresponding power relations are used to find or check mean proportionals; the text uses these relations to move between products and powers in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transference of proportionality by multiplying/dividing terms (testing by multiples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportional relations can be tested or established by comparing integer multiples of terms: if suitable integer multiples of given terms coincide or produce known products, the proportional relation is confirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise often demonstrates proportionality by showing that multiplying one term by an integer yields the same result as multiplying another term by a different integer (examples use numbers like 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 1020 in computations). This procedural test is used to verify or construct proportional sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic vs geometric (mechanical) methods to obtain intermediate means
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediate proportional terms may be obtained either by arithmetic computation (multiplication and root extraction) or by geometric construction/interpolation (compass/scale or mechanical-geometric methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author distinguishes algebraic/arithmetic procedures from geometric ones and notes that geometric constructions (compass, mechanical interpolation) can produce the same intermediate means when arithmetic extraction of roots is inconvenient. Both approaches are presented as valid depending on available tools and desired mode (arithmetical or geometrical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension and uniqueness of sequences from given terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Given some initial terms (extremes or some consecutive terms), one can uniquely determine other terms of a continued-proportional sequence by the rules (multiplication and root extraction or by repeated proportional construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains procedures for starting with two or three terms and extending the sequence forward or backward, often by multiplying and partitioning products appropriately. Numerical demonstrations show how starting with given terms leads to uniquely determined intermediate or further terms in the chain of proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum and grouping relations within continued proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums of particular groupings of continued-proportional quantities themselves satisfy proportional relations analogous to the original sequence; grouping and summing terms can be used in computations and verifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the exposition the author groups and sums various terms (e.g., sum of first several terms, sum of particular paired terms) and shows how these sums relate proportionally, using them as tools in examples and to simplify checking or producing proportionalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rules for generating tables of proportional quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: A systematic method is given to produce long lists/tables of proportional quantities by iterated multiplication, partitioning, and application of the previously stated proportional laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise demonstrates how to iterate the basic proportional operations (doubling, quadrupling, multiplying by powers) to fill extensive tables of proportional numbers (many numeric rows appear in the text). This is a practical algorithmic guidance for generating proportional data for examples or applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of proportionality through cross-relations (products of terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportional relations can be verified by comparing cross-products of terms (a·d = b·c for a:b = c:d in the two-term proportion case), extended appropriately to longer continued-proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although often presented as equal consecutive ratios, the equivalent check using cross-products is used in computations and examples to show that constructed terms indeed satisfy the proportional relations; this algebraic identity underpins many of the arithmetic verifications in the text.
